take: Hormuz risk is the dominant story: despite US claims that Iranian sea mines have been cleared from shipping lanes, the IMO confirms at least 70 attacks on ships since the conflict began, yet oil still lost 5% on the week as traders bet Tehran's control of the strait remains intact. The red-hot VLCC market is the second theme, with Frontline locking four ships into term charters at up to $120,000 per day and Saudi Arabia-to-China supertanker earnings at record highs, a direct transmission of war risk premia into freight rates. On flows, the $330 billion swell in the global energy import bill since March underscores how physical buyers are absorbing the conflict premium, whilst the US exploring an 18th-century law to seize and sell Iranian oil signals potential supply-side disruption to watch. Cross-market, the record VLCC earnings and Himalaya's fixed-rate cover at $53,000/day for newcastlemaxes highlight how tanker and dry bulk markets are both pricing in extended voyage times and rerouting around Hormuz, with product tanker newbuilds from Ardmore and Furetank adding to the supply-side response. Watch for any confirmation of actual tanker diversions away from Hormuz over the next 24 hours, as a break in the current trader conviction on Iranian resolve would trigger a sharp repricing of both crude and freight.
